title: Age pension spending set to drop
full_text:
Government spending on the age pension is set to shrink even as the nation's retirement age population doubles, Treasurer Jim Chalmers has revealed.
In a speech to the Super Members Council on September 9, Chalmers gave a "sneak peek" into the Intergenerational Report projections which showed the number of Australians over the age pension age will almost double to about nine million by 2066.
But he also revealed government spending on age and service pensions is projected to fall from 2.3 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) to 1.8 per cent in 2066 because of compounding superannuation balances.
"In comparison, that number is nearly 10 per cent by 2060 in the UK, 8 per cent in Canada, 7 per cent in New Zealand, and 6 per cent in the US," Chalmers said.
He added that if Australia's age pension expenditure remained at its current rate, the annual bill by 2066 would be $31 billion higher.
Compulsory super
The Treasurer used the speech to defend the compulsory superannuation system in the wake of One Nation's policy to allow workers to divert a quarter of their superannuation payments.
"Having super at the core of the best retirement incomes system in the world means pension spending as a share of the economy will be the lowest in the OECD but even as those costs moderate, retirees will have more economic security not less," Chalmers said. "Super takes serious pressure off social security outlays, and makes the budget much more sustainable as a consequence."
Chalmers forecast the median retirement age super balance is set to approach $450,000 over the next decade.
He used the speech to describe One Nation's super policy as "crazy" and questioned "supportive comments" from the Coalition.
"We're witnessing now the biggest threat to compulsory super, with preservation at its core, in the four decades since it began," he said.
The super debate
Under One Nation's plan workers would be able to divert 3 per cent, or a quarter of their total 12 per cent superannuation contributions, back into their bank accounts for up to three years.
"People are working hard and still struggling to get ahead," One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said. "If you take the boost, one quarter of this contribution will be paid directly to you by your super fund."
Liberal leader Angus Taylor has not backed the policy stating he did not want to change the way super was being paid. But Shadow Minister for Housing Andrew Bragg told News24 he had always been "skeptical" of Australia's superannuation scheme and endorsed letting people use their super to offset their mortgage.
New modelling
Meanwhile, modelling by the Super Members Council shows a median full-time worker withdrawing three per cent of contributions for three years would be $25,000 poorer by retirement.
A couple it would be more than $50,000 worse off.
"Turning super into an ATM is a reckless idea that would make battling Australians poorer," Super Members Council chief executive Misha Schubert said.
"This would belt battlers - not help them - by damaging their super and their retirements and driving up both inflation and interest rates which would make the cost-of-living pressures even worse, not better."
